The Vulcain test case has also been analyzed by a 1-D model, whose physical
and mathematical modeling is similar to the quasi-2-D model but the coolant velocity is constant in a channel section and the energy equation is not considered in the
2-D form of Eq. (16), but in the 1-D form of Eq. (12). This means that all the coolant
parameters vary only along the axial abscissa x and thus no thermal stratification
can be evaluated, as in a typical 1-D cooling channel flow model. For the 1-D flow
model, the same semiempirical expressions of the quasi-2-D model have been
adopted.

Wall heat flux from the hot-gas, coolant bulk temperature, wall temperature at
the hot-gas side, and coolant pressure are shown in Figure 7 for both 1-D and
quasi-2-D models. First, it has to be noticed that the discontinuity of the plots in
Figure 7 are due to the abrupt variation of the cooling channel cross-section (see
Figure 6), and to the mathematical formulation of Niino’s relation which has a different behavior in the cases of convex or concave curvature of the cooling channel.
In Figure 7a, the wall heat flux presents an evident peak value at the throat section
which is predicted to be 74 MW=m <sup>2</sup> in the case of the quasi-2-D model and only

64 MW=m <sup>2</sup> in the case of the 1-D model. The lower heat flux prediction is due to the
different modeling of the coolant flow; in fact, in the 1-D Approach the coolant is
characterized by a single temperature which is much higher than the bulk temperature predicted by the quasi-2-D model, as seen in Figure 7b, where the bulk temperature increase of the two models is shown to differ more than 50% at the channel exit.
The effect of the temperature stratification implies that the coolant far from the hot
wall remains cool, and thus it can absorb heat more efficiently; as a consequence, the
heat transfer is higher and the bulk temperature is lower. On the contrary, in the 1-D
model the description of the coolant by a single temperature (the bulk temperature)
leads to the underestimation of the coolant heat transfer capacity in the fluid regions
that are far from the hot wall. As a consequence, the wall temperature at the hot-gas
side predicted by the 1-D model is much higher than that predicted by the quasi-2-D
model (Figure 7c). Moreover, while the wall temperature values predicted by the 1-D
model are unrealistic, the maximum value being 1300 K, the quasi-2-D model shows
a wall temperature profile with values much closer to the expected ones, the
maximum values being located in the throat region and bounded between 850 K
and 900 K. This result is in good agreement with the experimental data of the
Vulcain engine thrust chamber [5], where the maximum wall temperature is nearly

800 K. Finally, Figure 7d shows the coolant pressure drop, which is 16.7 bar for the
quasi-2-D prediction and 26.4 bar for the 1-D prediction. The first result agrees quite
well with the prediction made in reference [6] with a parabolized Navier-Stokes equations solver, where the coolant pressure drop is evaluated as 16.2 bar; that is only a
3% discrepancy with the present prediction. These results confirm that the proposed
approach is able to describe the practical problem of a regenerative cooling system
far better than the popular 1-D approach.

6. CONCLUSION

A simplified model for the analysis of coolant flow evolution and of thermal
stratification in cooling channels has been developed and validated. The model
allows one to evaluate the radial thermal stratification both in the cooling channel
rib and in the coolant flow. Moreover, the introduction of a nonuniform velocity
profile in the coolant governing equations also permits to evaluate the behavior of
the heat flux from the rib to the coolant, whose description is of great importance
for evaluation, with reasonable accuracy, of the coupled wall-coolant problem.
The coolant flow model has been validated against CFD results of supercritical
methane in rectangular cooling channels; the comparison has shown good agreement
of the quasi-2-D model with the reference solution in the case of high aspect ratio
cooling channels, essentially because the rib heat transfer and friction force, which
are described by a 2-D radial model, are predominant to those of the base, which
are described by a less accurate 1-D model. The good agreement has been verified
on bulk variables (coolant pressure and temperature) and on variables in the radial
direction (coolant temperature and velocity). Then, the hot-gas=wall=coolant
coupled problem of the Vulcain rocket engine cooling system, which is characterized
by high aspect ratio cooling channels, has been analyzed in terms of wall heat flux
and temperature and on coolant pressure loss and temperature increase. The prediction of the quasi-2-D model has been compared to an equivalent 1-D model in which
the coolant behavior is described by a single temperature instead of a variable distribution in the radial direction. The comparison has shown that the quasi-2-D prediction is much more reliable than that of the 1-D model, thus giving confidence in the
description of the HARCC problem by means of the proposed approach. In fact,
quasi-2-D results show good agreement with the available experimental data of
maximum wall temperature in the throat region and coolant pressure drop.
